documents.title: ACUTE consensus medical care of patients with severe anorexia nervosa

chunks.content: Introduction Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are leading causes of death worldwide, accounting for roughly one-third of global deaths [ ]. Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is a manifestation of coronary atherosclerosis and a marker of overall atherosclerotic plaque burden [ ]. Noninvasive CT-based quantification of CAC, known as the CAC score (CACS), is crucial for detecting the presence and assessing the severity of coronary atherosclerosis [ , ]. Electrocardiogram (ECG)-gated cardiac CT is the reference standard for CACS acquisition because ECG synchronization reduces cardiac motion artifacts and yields high-quality images [ ]. Recent advancements in computer technology and artificial intelligence (AI) have facilitated the development of methods for deriving CACS from non-gated chest CT scans. Non-gated CACS obviate the necessity for specialized scan protocols, avoid increasing the patient’s radiation dose, and offer desirable cost-effectiveness. Multiple studies have demonstrated a high degree of concordance between non-gated CACS and ECG-gated cardiac CT scans [ – ]. A recent meta-analysis [ ] shows that non-gated chest CT is effective in identifying incidental CAC and has significant implications for patient prognosis. However, several aspects of deep learning-based non-gated CACS (DL-CACS) models remain unclear. In particular, the influence of scanner manufacturer and acquisition parameters on DL-CACS accuracy is not well defined and may affect performance [ ], as variations in scanners and parameter settings can alter image characteristics, including the apparent size and density of calcifications, image noise, and cardiac motion artifacts, thereby impacting estimation accuracy. Our study intends to incorporate chest CT scans from different vendors with various scanning parameters. By utilizing manually ECG-gated CACS obtained by radiologists as the gold standard, we seek to investigate the influence of varying scanning parameters on the reliability of non-gated DL-CACS. Our objective is to determine the CT imaging standards required for the precise assessment of non-gated CACS, thereby offering reliable guidance for clinical practice. Materials and methods Study population This retrospective study received approval from the ethics committee of our hospital, with the requirement for written informed consent waived. The study cohort consisted of patients who underwent ECG-gated cardiac CT examinations at our institution between January 2020 and February 2021. Inclusion criteria: (1) Patients who had undergone a non-gated chest CT scan within 3 months before or after the ECG-gated cardiac CT. Exclusion criteria: (1) Patients who had previously undergone coronary artery stenting, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass grafting; (2) Patients with implanted artificial heart valves or other cardiac devices; (3) Patients with coronary artery anomalies; (4) Patients whose image quality was deemed inadequate for analysis; (5) Images that could not be processed by the AI system. After patient enrollment, clinical data were collected via the electronic medical record system, including age, sex, smoking history, and comorbidities such as hypertension, hyperlipemia, and diabetes. CT acquisition Non-contrast, ECG-gated coronary CACS was used as the gold standard. ECG-gated coronary CT was performed on a United Imaging uCT 960 (United Imaging Healthcare) and a GE Revolution scanner (GE Healthcare). For the uCT 960, a one-beat, free-breathing cardiac protocol was used, with scan mode selected according to heart rate (HR): free-breathing acquisition for HR ≤ 75 bpm and inspiratory breath-hold in the supine position for HR > 75 bpm. Scan parameters were: tube voltage, 100–120 kV; tube current modulation enabled; slice thickness, 0.5 mm; and phase selection stratified by HR (30–40% of the R–R interval for HR > 75 bpm; 60–80% for HR ≤ 75 bpm). All GE Revolution scans were acquired during inspiratory breath-hold in the supine position, covering from 2 cm below the aortic arch to the cardiac base. Scan parameters were: tube voltage, 100–120 kV; tube current modulation enabled; slice thickness, 0.625 mm; and acquisition phases identical to those used on the uCT 960. Non-gated chest CT was performed without HR control, covering from the lung apices to the diaphragmatic domes. Non-gated scans were acquired on 10 different scanner models from three major vendors (United Imaging Healthcare, GE Healthcare, and Siemens Healthineers).Recorded acquisition parameters included tube voltage (120 kVp, 100 kVp); collimation (small ≤ 20 mm, medium 21–50 mm, wide > 50 mm); rotation time (fast ≤ 0.35 s/rot, regular 0.36–0.60 s/rot, slow > 0.60 s/rot); pitch (regular ≤ 1.2, high-pitch > 1.2); reconstruction slice thickness (thin ≤ 1.25 mm, thick 5 mm); and reconstruction kernel (smooth, sharp, ultra-sharp). Detailed scanner-specific parameters are provided in Supplementary Table . CACS measurement CACS was assessed by a cardiac CT radiologist with 10 years of experience on vendor-specific workstations. Analyses for the United Imaging uCT 960 were performed on the uWS-CT post‑processing platform (United Imaging Healthcare), and those for the GE Revolution on an AW workstation (GE Healthcare). CACS measurement CACS was assessed by a cardiac CT radiologist with 10 years of experience on vendor-specific workstations. Analyses for the United Imaging uCT 960 were performed on the uWS-CT post‑processing platform (United Imaging Healthcare), and those for the GE Revolution on an AW workstation (GE Healthcare). Coronary calcium analysis followed the Agatston method [ ], with the density weighting factor assigned by peak attenuation as follows: 1 for 130–199 HU; 2 for 200–299 HU; 3 for 300–399 HU; and 4 for ≥ 400 HU. The score was calculated as follows: First, the software automatically identified candidate coronary calcifications with attenuation ≥ 130 HU and in-plane area ≥ 1.0 mm². The radiologist then reviewed the automatically labeled regions slice by slice, manually excluding non-coronary findings such as costal calcifications and vessel wall artifacts. The software used multicolor coding to visualize the distribution across the left main (LM), left anterior descending (LAD), left circumflex (LCX), and right coronary artery (RCA). Per-artery Agatston scores were summed to obtain the total Agatston score (TOTAL). According to the Society of Cardiovascular Computed Tomography (SCCT) Coronary Artery Calcium Data and Reporting System (CAC-DRS) [ ], CACS risk categories were defined as follows: CAC-DRS 0 (score 0; very low risk); CAC-DRS 1 (score 1–99; mildly increased risk); CAC-DRS 2 (score 100–299; moderately increased risk); and CAC-DRS 3 (score ≥ 300; moderately to severely increased risk). Non-gated CACS analysis was performed using the CACScoreDoc AI-based calcium scoring system (Shukun Technology). The system implements a fully automated 3D U‑Net–based pipeline, with the workflow shown in Fig. . First, the cardiac region was automatically localized and segmented in 3D from the input non-gated chest CT. Next, a multi-task convolutional neural network detected coronary calcifications and classified them by coronary branch. Morphological algorithms then quantified calcified-lesion volume and mass, and the CACS was computed by the Agatston method. Finally, the system generated a structured report including the calcium score, spatial heat maps, and risk stratification. Statistical analysis Normally distributed continuous variables were reported as mean ± standard deviation, and non‑normally distributed variables as median (interquartile range). Categorical variables were expressed as counts (percentages). Agreement between non‑gated and gated CACS was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Measurement differences were visualized with Bland–Altman plots, and the mean bias and 95% limits of agreement were calculated. Classification agreement for CAC‑DRS risk categories was evaluated using kappa coefficient. Diagnostic performance in distinguishing correct from incorrect CAC-DRS risk categorization was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with the area under the curve (AUC) calculated. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the impact of scan parameters on the accuracy of non‑gated CACS; missing data were handled by multiple imputation. Candidate predictors were selected using a stepwise procedure in which variables with P < 0.20 in univariate logistic regression were entered into the multivariable logistic regression model to estimate odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). All analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.0 and R version 4.2.0, and a two‑sided α of 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Study cohort From January 2020 to February 2021, a total of 1494 patients who underwent ECG-gated cardiac CT at our institution were assessed for eligibility. The study flow diagram is shown in Fig. . According to the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1213 patients were ultimately included in the study cohort, comprising 592 men and 621 women, with a mean age of 62.4 ± 12.5 years. Each patient provided three axial reconstruction series (thick-slice lung window, thin-slice lung window, and mediastinal window), for a total of 3639 series. Detailed characteristics of the study cohort are shown in Table . Correlation between non-gated and Gated CACS Spearman correlation demonstrated strong associations between non-gated and gated CACS across LM, LAD, LCX, RCA, and TOTAL: ρ = 0.689, 0.846, 0.744, 0.791, and 0.865, respectively (all p < 0.001). Bland–Altman plots showed the bias and the 95% limits of agreement between non-gated and gated CACS. Detailed Spearman correlations and Bland–Altman plots for each coronary branch and the total score are presented in Fig. . Agreement in CAC-DRS risk stratification, assessed using the kappa statistic, was κ = 0.641 ( p < 0.001), indicating substantial agreement. The detailed cross-tabulation of risk category assignments is shown in Supplementary Table S2. Impact of scan parameters on the accuracy of non-gated CACS The accuracy of non-gated CACS for CAC-DRS risk stratification was 77.5%. The detailed cross-tabulation of risk category assignments is shown in Supplementary Table S2. Impact of scan parameters on the accuracy of non-gated CACS The accuracy of non-gated CACS for CAC-DRS risk stratification was 77.5%. Figure shows the ROC curve, with an AUC of 0.769 (95% CI 0.754–0.785; p < 0.001). In univariable logistic regression, collimation, rotation time, pitch, reconstructed slice thickness, and reconstruction kernel were significantly associated with CAC-DRS misclassification ( p < 0.05). Other covariates, including age, sex, smoking history, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, tube voltage, and radiation dose, were not significantly associated ( p > 0.05); however, hypertension had p < 0.20 and was therefore included in the multivariable model. The multivariable logistic regression analysis showed that collimation, rotation time, reconstructed slice thickness, and reconstruction kernel were independent predictors of CAC-DRS misclassification, whereas hypertension and pitch were not significantly associated with misclassification. The results indicated that, compared with systems using wider collimation, those with narrower collimation had higher odds of CAC-DRS misclassification (OR 0.202; 95% CI 0.063–0.651; p = 0.007); slower rotation time was associated with higher odds of misclassification (OR 1.207; 95% CI 1.021–1.427; p = 0.027); greater reconstructed slice thickness was associated with higher odds (OR 2.901; 95% CI 2.314–3.637; p = 0.020); and, relative to a sharp reconstruction kernel, a smooth kernel was more likely to result in misclassification (OR 0.555; 95% CI 0.489–0.630; p < 0.001). Detailed univariable and multivariable results are provided in Table . The forest plot from the multivariable logistic regression (Fig. ) visually summarizes the associations between scan parameters and misclassification of CAC-DRS. Discussion The global burden of CVD is substantial, and it remains a leading cause of death worldwide [ ]. CACS is a key metric for assessing atherosclerosis and stratifying cardiovascular risk [ – ]. It is conventionally obtained from ECG-gated cardiac CT, and its use is endorsed by multiple CAD guidelines [ , ]. A substantial proportion of coronary deaths occur in asymptomatic individuals, underscoring the need for early, population-level identification. Opportunistic AI-based CACS from routine chest CT can broaden screening without additional radiation or cost, offering meaningful clinical utility. We found that DL-based non-gated chest CT calcium scoring closely matched the gated reference: total correlation ρ = 0.865 with strong branch-level correlations; CAC-DRS agreement κ = 0.641, risk-category accuracy 77.5%, and AUC 0.769—consistent with prior reports [ – ]. However, previous investigations rarely stratified by scanner vendor and model when assessing non-gated CACS accuracy, potentially overlooking hardware- and parameter-related heterogeneity. In clinical practice, chest CT parameters vary considerably across institutions, influencing apparent calcification size and density, image noise, and cardiac motion artifacts, and thereby affecting CACS accuracy. Therefore, clarifying the effects of scanner type and scan parameters on the accuracy of DL-driven, non-gated CACS is essential for developing generalizable imaging and algorithmic strategies, reducing misclassification, and optimizing clinical decision-making. In multivariable logistic regression, collimation, rotation time, reconstruction slice thickness, and reconstruction kernel emerged as independent predictors of risk‑stratification misclassification for non‑gated CACS, whereas tube voltage, radiation dose, and pitch were not statistically significant. A smaller collimation width was significantly associated with a higher risk of misclassification. From a technical perspective, although narrower collimation can theoretically mitigate partial‑volume effects by improving longitudinal resolution, thereby facilitating the detection of small calcifications [ ], in the context of non‑gated scanning it is often accompanied by prolonged scan time (or may necessitate a higher pitch), which increases the likelihood and severity of cardiac motion artifacts [ ]. Such artifacts blur calcification boundaries and reduce apparent attenuation, leading to segmentation errors or misses; these, in turn, interfere with AI‑based detection and quantification and ultimately compromise the accuracy of risk stratification. CT rotation time is a key determinant of temporal resolution. In this study, scanners with longer rotation times were associated with higher rates of risk‑stratification misclassification. Longer rotation times widen the per‑slice acquisition window and, under non‑gated conditions, exacerbate motion blur arising from cardiac contraction and respiratory motion [ ]. The principal consequences are: (1) blurred calcification boundaries, increasing uncertainty in AI segmentation; (2) greater fluctuation in CT attenuation within calcified regions, impairing accurate assignment of the density factor; and (3) reduced detection of small calcifications. Collectively, these effects degrade AI model performance for detection and evaluation. Reconstruction slice thickness refers to the thickness of the reconstructed volume along the z-axis and directly affects spatial resolution and partial volume effects. In this study, greater reconstruction slice thickness was associated with significantly higher odds of misclassification, consistent with prior studies [ ]. Thinner slices provide higher through-plane spatial resolution and clearer visualization of small calcifications, while also mitigating partial volume effects. Reconstruction slice thickness refers to the thickness of the reconstructed volume along the z-axis and directly affects spatial resolution and partial volume effects. In this study, greater reconstruction slice thickness was associated with significantly higher odds of misclassification, consistent with prior studies [ ]. Thinner slices provide higher through-plane spatial resolution and clearer visualization of small calcifications, while also mitigating partial volume effects. Conversely, with thicker slices, small (< 1 mm) or low-density (130–200 HU) calcifications may not reach a threshold of ≥ 130 HU because of partial volume averaging with adjacent soft tissue. As a result, AI-based segmentation may underestimate the extent and density of calcified regions, ultimately yielding lower Agatston scores and underestimating CAC-DRS risk categories. Image reconstruction kernels are filtering functions applied during image reconstruction from projection data—implemented in the frequency or spatial domain—to balance spatial resolution against noise and to shape edge sharpness, texture, and contrast characteristics [ ]. In our study, with the sharp kernel as the reference, use of a smooth kernel was associated with risk-stratification misclassification. This result differs from the findings reported by Sun et al. [ ], who found lower image noise, higher signal-to-noise and contrast-to-noise ratios, and the lowest proportion of CACS misclassification under non–ECG-gated conditions when smooth kernels were used. These findings were attributed to the substantial impact of motion artifacts on CACS measurements in the absence of ECG gating and the notion that smooth kernels facilitate discrimination of artifacts arising from cardiac motion, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy. We note that reconstruction kernels primarily differ in their frequency responses and do not intrinsically mitigate motion artifacts. The principal effect of smooth kernels is to suppress high-frequency noise and enhance the conspicuity of low-contrast structures; however, they simultaneously attenuate edge sharpness of high-contrast targets such as coronary calcifications and may lower peak attenuation. Consequently, AI-based segmentation may blur boundary delineation and underestimate lesion density, resulting in systematic underestimation of Agatston scores. By contrast, sharp kernels better preserve edge and attenuation information of calcifications, improving AI-based detection and quantification. CT pitch is defined as the ratio of table travel per rotation to the nominal slice thickness, or, in some systems, to the total detector coverage, and reflects the trade-off between sampling density and scan speed. In our study, pitch was significantly associated with the outcome in univariable logistic regression but was not independently associated in multivariable analysis. This pattern may indicate that its effect is overshadowed by other motion-related parameters, such as rotation time, or that the interrelationships among pitch, scan speed, and coverage vary across scanners and protocols, thereby obscuring its independent effect in our cohort. The specific impact of pitch on non–ECG-gated CACS warrants further investigation using standardized acquisition protocols and rigorous control of confounders, including harmonized rotation time, slice thickness, and reconstruction kernels. Notably, a small number of cases exhibited clinically significant false positives, where non-gated DL-CACS indicated substantial calcium burden while the reference gated CACS was 0. These errors are likely attributable to non-coronary structures (e.g., rib calcifications, aortic wall calcification, or pericardial tissues) being misidentified as coronary calcium, particularly in the presence of image noise or motion artifacts. These observations underscore the importance of continued algorithm refinement to improve specificity. To our knowledge, this is the first study to systematically evaluate the impact of CT scanner models and acquisition parameters on DL‑CACS accuracy. We developed a multivariable modeling framework to assess the independent effects of key acquisition parameters and their interactions on measurement accuracy. Prior work has focused on agreement between non–ECG‑gated and ECG‑gated CACS [ – ], with limited evaluation of how acquisition parameters influence accuracy. Studies that considered acquisition factors largely examined single‑parameter effects [ , ] and lacked systematic multivariable analysis. In clinical practice, protocol variability can affect accuracy; in our cohort, collimation, rotation time, reconstruction slice thickness, and reconstruction kernel were associated with DL‑CACS performance. Algorithm development and validation should explicitly account for these factors, and clinical reports should document key acquisition and reconstruction parameters. These findings support parameter optimization; with protocol standardization and iterative model refinement, DL‑CACS could serve as a reliable tool for cardiovascular risk stratification.This study has several limitations. First, it is a single-center retrospective study, which may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability; multicenter prospective studies are needed for external validation. Second, although we included 10 chest CT scanners from multiple vendors, coverage of acquisition-parameter combinations was uneven, with uncommon combinations insufficiently represented. Third, the endpoints were agreement with ECG-gated CACS and CAC-DRS–based risk-stratification accuracy; prognostic validation with cardiovascular events was not performed, and the incremental value of non–ECG-gated CACS for prediction and clinical decision-making requires confirmation in longitudinal studies. First, it is a single-center retrospective study, which may introduce selection bias and limit generalizability; multicenter prospective studies are needed for external validation. Second, although we included 10 chest CT scanners from multiple vendors, coverage of acquisition-parameter combinations was uneven, with uncommon combinations insufficiently represented. Third, the endpoints were agreement with ECG-gated CACS and CAC-DRS–based risk-stratification accuracy; prognostic validation with cardiovascular events was not performed, and the incremental value of non–ECG-gated CACS for prediction and clinical decision-making requires confirmation in longitudinal studies. Fourth, the findings are based on a single deep learning model and a fixed pipeline; differences in architecture, training data, and post-processing may yield model-specific sensitivity to acquisition parameters, limiting generalizability across models and settings. Fifth, while we included all three reconstruction series from each patient to provide a comprehensive assessment across clinically relevant image types, we recognize that these observations are not strictly independent due to originating from the same raw CT data. This trade-off reflects our priority of evaluating DL-CACS performance across the full spectrum of clinically encountered image reconstructions. Beyond the specific limitations of this study, the deep learning-based non-ECG-gated CACS technique itself has inherent advantages and disadvantages. Its primary advantage lies in its opportunistic nature, enabling coronary calcium assessment from routine chest CT without additional radiation, contrast, or dedicated ECG-gated acquisitions, offering significant potential for large-scale cardiovascular risk stratification. However, several notable disadvantages warrant consideration. First, as demonstrated in this study, accuracy remains sensitive to variations in acquisition parameters and scanner models, which can lead to misclassification and limit cross-institutional generalizability. Second, in the absence of ECG gating, cardiac motion artifacts are unavoidable and can blur calcification boundaries, potentially compromising detection of small or low-density lesions. Third, current deep learning models are typically trained on data from specific scanner types and protocols, raising concerns about performance degradation when applied to out-of-distribution data. Finally, the lack of standardized protocols for non-gated CACS acquisition and reporting across institutions poses challenges for consistent clinical implementation and interpretation. Conclusion Non–ECG-gated chest CT with DL enables generally accurate CACS assessment, yet accuracy is sensitive to acquisition parameters. Smaller collimation width, slower rotation time, thicker slices, and smoother reconstruction kernels were associated with higher misclassification risk in risk stratification. In the future, improvements in scan protocols, algorithmic robustness across domains, and workflow standardization with quality control may further enhance the clinical utility of non–ECG-gated CACS.
